prompt:
Quicksort with uniform random pivots runs on n distinct elements. Name them in sorted order:

```formula
z_1 < z_2 < … < z_n
where
z_1, z_2, z_n: the smallest, second-smallest and largest elements
n: the number of elements
<: is less than
…: and so on, every element in sorted order
In words: z with subscript i is the i-th smallest element.
```

What is the probability that z₃ and z₇ are **ever compared**? Assume fresh independent uniform pivots and one comparison between each pivot and every other element in its partition.

options.explanation: There are more than two elements that could be chosen first from the block z₃..z₇.
The relevant set is only the block between them, not the whole array. Elements outside the block don't affect whether z₃ and z₇ are compared.
The pair is compared if the first pivot from the block is *either* endpoint, so there are two favourable choices, not one.
Correct. The block z₃..z₇ has 5 elements. They are compared only if z₃ or z₇ is the first of the block to be a pivot: 2 out of 5 equally likely choices.

workedExample:
1. The block between them is z₃, z₄, z₅, z₆, z₇: 5 elements.
2. All five stay in the same subarray until one of them becomes a pivot.
3. If that first pivot is z₄, z₅ or z₆, it separates z₃ and z₇ forever.
4. If it is z₃ or z₇, that pivot is compared with everything in its subarray, including the other.
5. Each of the five is equally likely to be first:

```formula
P(X_ij = 1) = 2 / (j − i + 1)
P(X_37 = 1) = 2 / (7 − 3 + 1) = 2/5
where
i, j: the ranks of the two elements, here 3 and 7
X_ij: the indicator that z_i and z_j are ever compared
X_37: the indicator for z_3 and z_7
j − i + 1: the size of the block from z_i to z_j, here 5
2: the two endpoints, the only first pivots that cause a comparison
P: probability; probabilities are dimensionless and apply to measurable events
In words: 2 of the 5 equally likely first pivots in the block lead to a comparison.
```

Adding the comparison probabilities across all unordered pairs gives the expected total; its leading term is twice the array length times its natural logarithm.

prompt: Which statements about **randomised** quicksort (uniformly random pivot) on an array of n elements are true? Select all that apply. Assume distinct keys, one pivot comparison per other element, and a fixed input independent of fresh uniform pivot choices.

options.text: Its expected number of comparisons is O(n log n) for every input, including sorted arrays
options.explanation: Correct. The expectation is over the algorithm's own random choices, so no input is bad on average.

options.text: Its maximum running time over pivot choices is still O(n²)
options.explanation: Correct. Terribly unlucky pivots can still produce quadratic time, though the probability is astronomically small for large arrays.

options.text: An attacker who knows the algorithm can craft an input that makes it slow every time
options.explanation: Under the stated fixed-input and independent-uniform-pivot assumptions, no fixed ordering forces quadratic work on every run. Predictable randomness or adaptive comparisons falls outside that model.

options.text: It is a Monte Carlo algorithm because it might return an unsorted array
options.explanation: It always sorts correctly; only the time varies. That makes it Las Vegas.

options.text: Each pair of elements is compared no more than once
options.explanation: Correct. Comparisons are between a pivot and other elements, and a pivot is excluded from all later recursive calls.

workedExample:
Separate *what is random* from *what is guaranteed* (n is the number of elements; O( ) is big-O, "grows at most as fast as"):

| Claim | Status |
|---|---|
| expected time O(n log n), any input | true |
| maximum over pivot choices O(n²) | true, rarely |
| attackable by input | no |
| may be wrong | no (Las Vegas) |
| pair compared no more than once | true |

The 'no more than once' fact is what lets the indicator proof work: total comparisons equal the number of pairs ever compared.
